Inﬂuence of oil content on physicochemical properties and skin distribution of Nile
red-loaded NLC
Veerawat Teeranachaideekul a,b, Prapaporn Boonme c, Eliana Barbosa Souto b,d,
Rainer Helmut Müller b, Varaporn Buraphacheep Junyaprasert a,⁎
a Department of Pharmacy, Faculty of Pharmacy, Mahidol University, Thailand
b Department of Pharmaceutics, Biopharmaceutics & Quality Management, Free University of Berlin, Germany
c Department of Pharmaceutical Technology, Faculty of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Prince of Songkla University, Thailand
d Department of Pharmaceutical Technology, Faculty of Health Sciences, Fernando Pessoa University, Portugal
article info abstract
Article history:
Received 10 October 2007
Accepted 20 February 2008
Available online 4 March 2008
The aims of this study were to investigate the effect of the oil content on the physicochemical properties of
NLC and to elucidate the potential of NLC for skin targeting. The obtained results showed that an increase in
the oil content did not affect the mean particle size of NLC but impacted on the zeta potential. The inner
structure of NLC was in ﬂuenced by the increasing proportion of oil towards the less ordered structure as
conﬁrmed by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and X-ray diffraction (XRD), particularly for the higher
medium chain triglycerides (MCT) loading. The data from proton nuclear magnetic resonance (
1H NMR)
revealed that cetyl palmitate nanoparticles did not completely recrystallize after cooling down to room
temperature.
1H NMR and DSC results indicate that MCT molecules were restricted in the NLC as compared to
the nanoemulsions (NE). Nile red distribution and penetration into skin from NLC were pronounced as
compared to NE and dependent on the MCT loading. The deep penetration and high amount of Nile red were
related to the occlusion factor. Moreover, the epidermal targeting was achieved by NLC applications,
particularly those containing 5% MCT (NLC-5) depending on the amount of MCT loading.

1. Introduction
Colloidal carrier systems based on lipid nanoparticles, so-called
solid lipid nanoparticles (SLN) and nanostructured lipid carriers (NLC),
have been intensively studied as drug delivery systems for several
routes of administration such as peroral, parenteral, dermal and topical
delivery [1–5]. SLN are prepared from a solid lipid, e.g. a highly pure
lipid (e.g. tristearin) or a less de ﬁned mixture of acylglycerols (e.g.
Compritol® and Imwitor ®) whereas NLC are produced from a lipid
blend, consisting of a mixture of a solid lipid with oil. SLN and NLC are
both prepared using biodegradable and biocompatible lipids [6–8].
The lipid nanoparticles have shown several advantages, e.g. ease of
large scale production, avoiding the use of organic solvents, feasibility
of achieving controlled drug release and drug targeting [8,9].
With respect to the skin delivery, several studies have been focused
on the suitability of SLN as a carrier for drug targeting. In previous
studies using Franz diffusion cells, it has been reported that retinol,
isotretinoin, glucocorticoids, and podophyllotoxin encapsulated into
SLN showed a good skin targeting [10–14]. Applying confocal laser
scanning microscopy (CLSM), it has also been reported that SLN were a
preferential drug delivery with regard to their higher drug penetration
through the skin in comparison to NLC and nanoemulsions (NE) of
similar composition [15]. These properties were explained by the lipid
modiﬁcation of the SLN matrix leading to the drug expulsion and
subsequently to the enhancement of drug penetration into pig skin
[15,16]. On the other hand, encapsulation of ﬂuorescence dye into SLN
was alike in dye uptake regardless the type of solid lipids. In the same
study, NLC dispersions prepared using different oils, also did not show
any differences in dye uptake [15].
In different studies, NLC prepared varying the solid lipid and oil
ratio showed signi ﬁcant differences in the in vitro release pro ﬁles
when investigated by Franz diffusion cell using cellulose as a
membrane [17–20]. NLC with a higher oil ratio revealed a higher
drug release in comparison to NLC composed of lower oil ratio and to
SLN (100% solid lipid). Similar ﬁndings were also reported by Souto
et al. for clotrimazole-loaded SLN and NLC [21]. It can be therefore
concluded that the release pro ﬁle of the drug incorporated into NLC
can be modulated by varying the ratios between solid lipid and oil
composition. Nonetheless, the effect of such ratio changes in NLC
formulations on the skin penetration and distribution of the entrapped
drug has not been investigated yet. Major studies have been focused on
the effect of varying the lipid composition on the physicochemical
properties of the particles, e.g. particle size, zeta potential, and
crystallinity [17–20].
CLSM is a well-established technique for visual investigation of the
skin both in vitro and in vivo , with several advantages, e.g. non-

The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of the amount of MCT
(oil) on the physicochemical properties, skin distribution and penetration
of Nile red-loaded NLC composed of cetyl palmitate as a solid lipid. The
amount of MCT varied from 5% up to 100% in reference nanoemulsion of
similar composition, and 0.05% of Nile red (with regard to the lipid matrix)
was incorporated into the NLC due to its lipophilic character.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
Sabowax CP
® (cetyl palmitate) was obtained from Polygon Chemie
AG (Olten, Switzerland). Miglyol® 821 (Medium chain triacylglycerols,
MCT) were purchased from Gattefossé (Cedex, France) and Tego® Care
450 (Polyglyceryl-3 methylglucose distearate) from Goldschmidt
(Essen, Germany). Nile red and methanol were obtained respectively
from Sigma Aldrich and Merck (Deisenhofen, Germany), respectively.
Sterile water for injection was obtained from a General Hospital
Products (Bangkok, Thailand). All chemical were pharmaceutical
grade and used without further modi ﬁcation.
2.2. Preparation of NLC and NE
NLC containing 0.005% of Nile red in the formulation with various
ratios of cetyl palmitate and MCT were produced by hot high pressure
homogenization (HPH) using an EmulsiFlex-C3 (Avestin, Canada). Brieﬂy,
the melted lipid phase containing solid lipid, oil and Nile red was
dispersed in a hot surfactant solution (85 °C) to produce a pre-emulsion
by high speed stirring using an Ultra-Turrax T25 (IKA-Werke, Germany)
at 8000 rpm for 1 min. This hot pre-emulsion was further processed by
HPH applying 1 homogenization cycle at 500 bar and 85 °C. The lipid
dispersion was cooled down at ambient conditions to room temperature
and solidi ﬁed to obtain the aqueous NLC dispersions. In the case of
nanoemulsions, the same manufacturing procedure was applied; none-
theless, in this case the solid lipid (cetyl palmitate) was replaced by MCT.
2.3. Particle size analysis
The mean particle size ( z-ave) and the polydispersity index (PI)
were determined by photon correlation spectroscopy (PCS) using a
Malvern Nanosizer ZS (Malvern Instruments, UK). The detection optics
was set at position of 1 73° to reduce the effects of multiple scattering
where the scattered light from one particle is itself scattered by the
other particles. Prior to the measurement, the samples were diluted
with double distilled water to a suitable scattering intensity. The
particle sizes were computed using Stokes –Einstein equation:
D ¼ kT

where D is the diffusion coef ﬁcient, k is the Boltzmann constant, T is
the absolute temperature, η is the viscosity of the dispersing liquid,
and d is the particle size diameter.
2.4. Zeta potential analysis
The zeta potential (ZP) is a measure of the electric charge at the
surface of the particles indicating the physical stability of colloidal
systems. The ZP values higher than |30 mV| indicate electrostatic long-
term stability of aqueous dispersions. In this study, the ZP values were
assessed by determining the particle electrophoretic mobility using
the Malvern Nanosizer (Malvern Instruments, UK). The measurements
were performed in ultrapuri ﬁed water adjusted to a standardized
conductivity of 50 μS/cm by addition of sodium chloride solution (0.9%
w/v) to avoid changes in ZP values due to day-to-day variations
occurring in the conductivity of the water. The pH was in the range of
5.5–6.0. The ZP values were calculated using the Helmholtz –
Smoluchowski equation:
ZP ¼ 4mpg
Ee ð2Þ
where ZP is the zeta potential, ν is the particle velocity, η is the
viscosity of the dispersing medium, E is the ﬁeld strength and ε is the
dielectric constant.
2.5. Differential scanning calorimetry
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analysis was performed
using a Mettler DSC 823e apparatus (Mettler Toledo, Gie βen, Switzer-
land), and the aforementioned parameters were calculated by the
STARe Software. The sample weights were approximately 1 –2m g
based on the lipid contents of the NLC dispersions and placed in 40 μl
aluminum pans. The heating runs were performed from 25 °C to 85 °C
and cooled down to −60 °C at the heating/cooling rate of 5 K/min. An
empty aluminum pan was used as a reference. The CI [%] was calculated
applying the following equation:

2.6. X-ray diffraction
X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed using a wide-angle
X-ray scattering (WAXS, 2 Theta 10°–30°) on a Bruker AXS diffractometer
D8 (Karlsruhe, Germany) with a copper anode (Cu-Kα radiation, 40 kV,
25 mA, λ = 0.15406 nm), using a Goniometer Code 20 as a detector. Prior
to the measurement, 1 .0 ml of aqueous NLC dispersions was mixed with
0.4 g of locust bean gum powder so as to transform liquid NLC into a
paste. Afterwards, the samples were mounted onto a thin aluminum
holder prior to the analysis by WAXS. The obtained data were typically
collected with a step width of 0.04° and a count time of 3 s.
2.7. Proton nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy measurement
Proton nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy measurement
(1H NMR) spectra were recorded by an Avance 300, operating at
300 MHz and 25 °C. An aliquot of each aqueous nanodispersion was
ﬁlled in an NMR tube. Accurately weighed quantities of deuterized
water or chloroform-D1 were added for ﬁeld login and tetramethylsi-
lane (TMS) was added as a reference for 0 ppm.
2.8. Occlusive effects
In order to evaluate the effects of oil loading on the occlusive
properties of NLC, an in vitro occlusion test modi ﬁed after the de
Vringer method was performed [24]. Glass bottles (50 ml) with a
diameter of 35 mm were ﬁlled with 30 g of water and covered with a
ﬁlter paper (cellulose ﬁlters, 90 mm, Whatman number 6, cutoff size:
3 μm, USA). 300 μl of sample was spread homogeneously with a spatula
on the ﬁlter surface (9.63 cm 2) and the sample was subsequently
stored at 32 °C for 48 h in order to mimic the temperature of the skin
surface. The weight of water remaining in the glass bottles was
weighed at 8, 24, and 48 h. The glass bottles covered with the ﬁlter
paper which was spread with water was used as a reference. All

2.9. Distribution of ﬂuorescence dye study
2.9.1. Skin preparation
Excised human skin samples were obtained from abdominoplastic
surgeries from females with age ranging from 25 to 45 years old. The
excess adipose layer was sectioned off from the received tissues by
surgical scissors. The skin was then wrapped in the aluminum foil and
stored at – 20 °C until use. Prior to the experiment, the frozen skin was
thawed, cut into 4.5 × 4.5 cm2 pieces and hydrated by placing in isotonic
phosphate buffer (pH = 7 .4) overnight in a refrigerator (at about 4 °C). The
study was carried out with the approval of the Committee on Human
Rights Related to Human Experimentation, Mahidol University, Bang-
kok, Thailand.
2.9.2. Confocal laser scanning microscopy
In order to investigate the effects of oil loading on the distribution
of ﬂuorescence dye in the skin by CLSM, 0.005% Nile red-loaded NLC
with various amounts of oil, i.e. 5, 10, 30, 50, and 100% (NE, reference
nanoemulsion) were prepared. Nile red distribution in the different
skin layers was investigated using CLSM (FluoView FV1000 with IX2
inverted microscope: Helium –Neon red exciting wavelengths of
543 nm). The emission wavelength was at 578 nm. The images were
recorded by setting the camera integration time to 10 ms. Sample
speed was 4.0 µS/Pixel. The objective lens was in the magni ﬁcation of
20× (Olympus, microscope, Japan).
In this study, the mixture of phosphate buffer pH 7 .4 and methanol at
the ratios of 70 and 30 (%v/v) was used as an acceptor medium to achieve
the sink condition during the experiment due to the high solubility of
Nile red in methanol. After applying Nile red-loaded NLC and NE
dispersions on the skin surface, at 3 and 9 h the dye was carefully
removed by cotton bud and the skin was rinsed with distilled water.
Then, the treated skins were removed from the Franz diffusion cells. The
skin was frozen afterwards by immersion in liquid nitrogen and cut from
dermis to stratum corneum side (vertical slices) with the thickness of
50 μm. Each sample was cut into 3 slices and 3 different areas of each
slice were recorded. All preparations were tested using the human skin
obtained from three donors.
The skin slices were investigated under both normal light and
ﬂuorescence microscopes. The images from the two techniques were
overlaid to obtain the information of the Nile red distribution in the
different skin layers.
2.9.3. Statistical analysis
The data were calculated as the mean value ± standard deviation (S.D.).
Signiﬁcance of difference was evaluated using Student'st-test and one-
way ANOVA with Turkey HSD at the probability level of 0.05.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Preparation of Nile red-loaded NLC and NE formulations
In this study, the total amount of lipid phase (cetyl palmitate and
MCT) was kept constant being 10% with regard to the total
formulation, while the ratio between solid lipid (cetyl palmitate)
and oil (MCT) varied, i.e. from a percentage of 5% to 100% MCT in the
particles, 100% being the NE. After production, it was found that the
particle size of all Nile red-loaded NLC dispersions was higher than
that of Nile red-loaded NE ( p b 0.05). Nonetheless, the effect of oil
loading did not signi ﬁcantly in ﬂuenced the particle size of NLC
(p N 0.05) ( Table 1 ). The mean particle size of lipid nanoparticles
usually depends on several factors, e.g. type and concentration of
lipids and surfactants, and the viscosity of the lipid phase.
Concerning the production process of NLC, the lipid and aqueous
phases were heated up to 85 °C, thus the viscosity of the lipid phase
composed of different oil content should be nearly similar [25].A sa
result, all NLC formulations should provide the same mean particle
size. However, the particle size of NE determined by PCS was smaller
than that of NLC. This might be due to the characteristic anisometric
shape of NLC that leads to different diffusion coef ﬁcient ( D) values
between spherical NE droplets and NLC, as previously described by
Jores et al. [25]. This phenomenon directly affected the mean particle
size computed by Stokes –Einstein equation (Eq. (1)) which was used
to calculate the mean particle size by PCS. Comparing in the same
sample volume the D values of the spherical NE and the anisometric
NLC, the former ones were higher than the latter. With respect to the
Stokes–Einstein equation (Eq. (1)), the higher the D values, the
smaller the particle size was. Recently, it was reported that the
particle size of NLC based on monocaprate and MCT mixtures
depended on the content of oil loading. Increasing the oil content up
to 20% led to an increase of the particle size, while it decreased
dramatically when the oil content achieved up to 30%. This was
attributed to the expulsion of the excess of oil during the lipid
crystallization process. Nonetheless, this phenomenon may depend
on many factors, such as the chemical structure of the lipids used, as
well as their chemical interaction [26]. From the production of NE by
HPH, it is known that the droplet size is increased with increasing
viscosity of the oil phase. The viscosity of the melted blend of cetyl
palmitate and MCT is de ﬁnitely higher than the one of pure MCT,
being considered as the most important factor for the larger size of
the NLC.
ZP values of all developed formulations are shown in Table 1 .
Because of the negative charged MCT at their carboxylic groups, NE
revealed the highest ZP values. The ZP values of NLC increased
with the increase of an oil loading. This might be due to the
accumulation of MCT at the surface of the NLC. In fact, the melting
point of cetyl palmitate is obviously higher than that of MCT
(~ 50 °C versus ~ ( − 1 °C)). Consequently, when preparing NLC by hot
HPH, the lipid core of the particles – composed of MCT dissolved in
the melted cetyl palmitate – starts recrystallizing ﬁrst being
therefore entrapped within the solid lipid matrix. Subsequently,
the excess of MCT will be accumulated in the outer shell of the
nanoparticles, similarly to the drug-enriched shell model proposed
as one of the drug encapsulation models for SLN [6]. A similar
description has been proposed for the coenzyme Q
10-loaded NLC
composed of cetyl palmitate and MCT as lipid matrix [19].T h e
occurrence of such model has been proven by an in vitro release
study using formulations prepared with different ratios of oil and
solid lipid. The higher the oil loading, the higher the drug release
was [19].

3.2. DSC investigations
Fig. 1A shows the DSC curves of Nile red-loaded NLC composed of
different oil contents. Table 2 shows the DSC parameters of all
developed NLC dispersions recorded from 20 °C to 85 °C at a heating
run of 5 K/min. All NLC dispersions showed a melting peak indicating
the presence of a solid state and the occurrence of supercooled melts
could be excluded. In comparison to the bulk cetyl palmitate, both the
melting point and enthalpy of all NLC formulation decreased. The ﬁrst
heating run recorded for the bulk cetyl palmitate revealed the peak
maximum at 49.23 °C, but two melting endothermic events were
recorded in the second heating run of the solid lipid, i.e. at 48.35 °C and
38.54 °C ( Fig. 1 B). This means that the heating process affected the
polymorphism of the bulk cetyl palmitate. However, DSC curves of the
ﬁrst and second cooling runs were similar indicating that recrystalliza-
tion process was not disturbed by the heating process. The peak
maximum of bulk cetyl palmitate decreased from 49.23 °C to 46.86 °C
when the lipid was formulated as SLN (0% MCT). Such decrease in the
melting point can be explained by the small particle size in the
nanometer range, the higher speciﬁc surface area, and by the presence of
surfactants[27 ,28]. The melting point depression owing to the reduction
of particle size to the nanosize range can be attributed to the Kelvin
effect which is described by the Thomson equation [27]. Furthermore,
increasing the MCT content led to the decrease of melting peak and
melting enthalpy as well. With respect to the melting endotherms of
NLC, they were composed of two peaks that could be compared to the
second heating run of the bulk cetyl palmitate. Besides, the melting
isotherm decreased almost linearly with the increase in the MCT content
in the NLC. From Fig. 1A, it was noticeable that the increase in MCT
content resulted in broad melting endotherms meaning that the oil
incorporation avoided or delayed the recrystallization of the lipid matrix
during the cooling process. Comparing the mean particle sizes of NLC-5,
NLC-10, NLC-30, and NLC-50, they were of the same order of magnitude.
Therefore, the difference in melting point due to the effect of differences
in particle size was excluded. The decrease of the melting point and
enthalpy (indicated by CI [%]), as well as the occurrence of broad peaks
indicate the presence of lattice defects (i.e. less ordered structure) or of a
partially recrystallization process of cetyl palmitate-based NLC, particu-
larly for the NLC with the highest MCT content (50% w/w) as conﬁrmed
by
1H NMR (discussed in 1H NMR section).
The polymorphism of MCT within the NLC matrices was also
investigated using DSC. Samples of the developed NLC and NE
formulations, and of MCT solely, were cooled down to – 60 °C at the
cooling rate of 5 K/min ( Fig. 1C). The crystallization temperatures of
solely MCT during the cooling process were −29.80 °C, −40.00 °C,
−43.50 °C, and −53.1 7 °C. In general, the main polymorphic forms of
triacylglycerols (TAG) are the α, β′,a n d β forms [29]. Moreover, an
intermediate form, namely βi, has also been reported [6,29,30].T h e r e -
fore, the crystallization peaks at−53.1 7 °C,−43.5 °C, −40 °C, and−29.5 °C
correspond to α, β′, βi and β forms, respectively. Upon the cooling
process of NLC and NE dispersions, the water crystallized between
−26 °C and −14 °C, followed by crystallization of the MCT. The
recrystallization of MCT from NE showed the similar patterns to that
of solely MCT. The data obtained based on NE were different from the
previously reported by Jenning et al. [20], which has been attributed to
the different surfactant used to stabilize the lipid formulations (e.g.
Poloxamer 188).
It was observed that the presence of a crystallization peak during
the cooling process of NLC depended on their MCT loading (Fig. 1C). As
compared to NE, the peak at approximately −30 °C corresponding to
the β form of NLC-5 was more pronounced than that recorded from
NLC-10, NLC-30 and NLC-50. Interestingly, the crystallization peaks of
NLC-50 were similar to those recorded for NE, nonetheless, NE peaks
were broader resulting from the less ordered structure of MCT in the

formulation. In fact, the increase in the melting range of MCT recorded
for NLC can be correlated with the creation of impurities and/or the
formation of a less ordered crystal structure of MCT during the cooling
of the lipid matrices [20]. Therefore, NLC-5 showed the lower mobility
of MCT molecules as shown by the narrow peak (i.e. −30 °C). The
obtained data are in agreement with the previous published results
for NLC based on glyceryl behenate and MCT [20] inferring that MCT in
the NLC should be in a higher ordered arrangement in comparison to
NE of similar composition. Moreover, the DSC data from both heating
and cooling runs are in line with the data obtained from the zeta
potential analysis. It could be, therefore, assumed that a part of the
MCT was included within the solid lipid matrices and the remaining
part accumulated in the outer shell or at the surface of NLC particles,
especially for the NLC with the higher MCT content.
3.3. X-ray diffraction investigations
WAXS analysis was performed to elucidate the effect of oil loading
on the subcell structures and polymorphism of cetyl palmitate. With
respect to the diffractogram of bulk lipid (cetyl palmitate), the typical
reﬂections at 0.38, 0.42 and 0.46 nm both before and after tempering
the samples at 85 °C for 1 h were observed ( Fig. 2 A). The half-line
width of the cetyl palmitate was lower after tempering than that
before tempering, meaning that temperature affects the crystallinity
of the lipid as con ﬁrmed by DSC.
Fig. 2B reveals the WAXS diffractograms of NLC-5, NLC-10, NLC-30,
and NLC-50. All developed NLC formulations (with different MCT
loadings) revealed the same re ﬂections at 0.38, 0.42 and 0.46 nm,
similarly to those of the bulk cetyl palmitate before and after
tempering, indicating that the presence of MCT within the system
did not change the polymorphism of cetyl palmitate. Nevertheless, the
peak intensity of NLC was less pronounced in comparison to that of
the bulk cetyl palmitate and decreased with the increase in MCT
content. Therefore, it could be emphasized that the degree of the less
ordered structure of NLC depends on the amount of MCT content. As
expected, no peak could be detected in the diffractograms of NE
indicating absence of MCT crystals (data not shown).
3.4.
1H NMR investigations
As described in the literature, the information about the mobility and
structure of lipid nanoparticles, e.g. SLN, NLC and NE can be obtained by
means of 1HN M R[20,27 ,31 ,32]. The mobility of the molecules is related
to the relaxation time indicated by the width of 1H NMR line, e.g.
decrease in mobility of molecules resulting in the broader lines of 1H
NMR. In order to compare the extent of immobilization of the molecules,
the widths at half height were measured. As expected, the spectrum of
cetyl palmitate in D 2O was not observed because the solid state (i.e.
restricted molecule) could not be detected due to a short relaxation time
(data not shown). Concerning the 1H NMR characteristics, the chemical
shifts of methyl (CH 3) and methylene (CH 2) protons are ~0.9 and
~1 .4 ppm. However, the positions of methyl and methylene protons in
MCT were affected by the glycerol part of MCT leading to deshield of
protons indicated by the increase in the proton chemical shift.
It was reported that SLN prepared from wax (cetyl palmitate) does
not completely recrystallize to a solid state at room temperature [33].
Retinol-loaded SLN based on cetyl palmitate displayed a high
tendency to form supercooled melts rather than the typical solid
particle matrix; however, the recrystallization of cetyl palmitate could
be induced by being stored at 4 °C for 24 h [33]. Therefore, the signal of
CH3 and CH 2 group from 1H NMR spectra may belong to both cetyl
palmitate and MCT. This could be proven by observing the ratio of CH 2
and CH 3 protons [34]. Due to the high solubility of MCT and cetyl
palmitate in CDCl 3, this solvent has been selected to demonstrate the
signal ratios of CH 2 and CH3 protons. The ratios of the area under the
curve of protons at ~ 1.4 and ~ 0.9 ppm of MCT and cetyl palmitate were
3.4 and 8.2, respectively.
Table 3 reveals the CH 2/CH3 ratios and widths at half height of
1H NMR at the position of ~ 1.4 ppm, of NLC and NE formulations
which were dispersed in the D 2O. It is clearly observed the higher
CH2/CH3 ratios of NLC formulations in comparison to NE, meaning
that the detected signals resulted from both liquid cetyl palmitate
and MCT.
Fig. 3 shows the major signals of CH 2 and CH 3 protons of all
developed NLC and NE formulations (black arrows). When compared
with NE, NLC showed similar patterns, yet the line widths at half
height were different. NLC showed the broader widths at half height,
depending on the MCT loading. It could be therefore concluded that
the CH2 and CH3 protons of liquid cetyl palmitate and MCT are strongly
restricted to the solid matrix of cetyl palmitate, especially in NLC-5.

increase of MCT content in NLC disturbs the inner structure of lipid
matrices indicated by the lower CI [%] and by the decrease of the peak

3.5. Occlusion factor
Fig. 4 compares the results obtained from the evaluation of
occlusiveness of NLC and NE formulations. The occlusion factor of NE
was lower than that of NLC, which was dependent on the MCT loading.
The occlusion factor of NLC-5 and NLC-10 was relatively high and the
differences in mean of occlusion factor observed at 8, 24, and 48 h
were not statistically signi ﬁcant ( p N 0.05); however, the increase of
MCT loading (NLC-30 and NLC-50) led to the decrease in the occlusion
factor. As a result, this factor might affect the bioavailability of the
drugs entrapped in NLC when administered topically. The occlusion
factor is dependent upon the sample volume, particle size, crystal-
linity, lipid concentration and type of colloidal systems [21,24]. In the
present work, NE were of smaller mean size than NLC ( Table 1 ).
Therefore, the higher occlusion factor observed for NLC is related the
solid state of the lipid matrix which can avoid the evaporation of water
through the ﬁlter paper. No signi ﬁcant differences in the particle size
were also found between NLC formulations, meaning that the effect of
particle size on NLC occlusiveness could also be excluded. Never-
theless, the data obtained from DSC and X-ray diffraction demon-
strated that the occlusion factor is related to the crystallinity and to
the peak intensity, i.e. the higher the crystallinity, the higher the
occlusion factor.

4. Conclusions
NLC formulations had been proven to be a suitable colloidal carrier
for epidermal targeting. The degree of epidermal targeting depended
on the MCT loading and on the occlusion factor. Moreover, the
increase of MCT loading in NLC did not change the polymorphism of
lipid matrices but rather disturbed the inner structures of NLC, as
indicated by the decrease of the enthalpy (DSC) and of the peak
intensity (X-ray diffraction). Moreover, the 1H NMR spectra revealed
that cetyl palmitate NLC did not completely recrystallize to a solid
state after cooling to room temperature but some parts remained in
the liquid state. In addition, 1H NMR and DSC results showed an
immobilization of MCT in the NLC matrices when compared to NE.
MCT was most likely to deposition at the particle surface when
incorporating high amounts of MCT in NLC, exceeding the amount of
MCT being dissolvable in the particle matrix. The physicochemical
properties and the degree of Nile red distribution were thus affected
by the varying ratio between solid lipid and oil in NLC.
